![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14215565/assets/4d81bebc6bb5addfdd5f9006eba8cd4b5e5a13c6322495a6af3c5c02885ae6ee.png)

The $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ on the curve $y={3}^{-x/4}$ that is closest to the origin (as shown above) satisfies the equation 

$$
2x-\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAA}}=0.
$$

 
What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
Let's consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(0,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x,y) & =(x-0)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={3}^{-x/4}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+({3}^{-x/4})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+{3}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot {3}^{-x/2} & =0 \\ 2x-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}\cdot {3}^{-x/2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$
